<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, PiliPala is a Flutter mobile application that acts as a third‐party BiliBili client. While it also includes project configurations for Android, iOS, web, desktop (macOS, Linux, Windows), the primary focus is on a mobile full-stack client. The project follows a layered separation: UI (pages and widgets), business logic (controllers, service locator, and plugins), data access (HTTP API calls and models), and platform-specific integrations.

Below are step-by-step guidelines for drawing a detailed and accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Frontend (Flutter UI)
     – The majority of the app’s presentation lives in the lib/pages directory, which is organized by features (e.g., home, video, dynamic, login, member, etc.)
     – lib/common also contains shared widgets and utility components.
   • Business Logic & State Management
     – Controllers inside each page directory orchestrate user interactions, data fetching, and navigation flows.
     – The project uses providers/service locators (see lib/services/service_locator.dart) for dependency management.
   • Data Access Layer
     – HTTP API communications are abstracted in lib/http (API endpoints for bangumi, dynamics, video, user, login, etc.).
     – Data models are well-organized in lib/models which mirror the domain objects that come from BiliBili APIs.
   • Plugins & Custom Modules
     – Custom plugins in lib/plugin (e.g., pl_gallery, pl_player, pl_popup, pl_socket) encapsulate reusable functionality like custom media viewing and socket communication.
   • Platform Integrations
     – Directories for android, ios, macos, linux, windows contain native project configurations and platform-specific code.
   • Assets & Resources
     – Assets folder holds fonts, images, and JSON files that support theming and media in the UI.
   • Build, CI/CD and Deployment
     – .github/workflows, fastlane and pubspec files indicate automated build and release processes.

2. Map Relationships and Interactions:
   • The UI Layer (lib/pages and lib/common/widgets) communicates with its corresponding controllers (in each feature’s controller.dart). Use arrows to indicate “User Interaction” and “Navigation Flow.”
   • Controllers call upon service classes in lib/services and HTTP helper classes (lib/http) to fetch data from external APIs (BiliBili official endpoints as mentioned in the README).
   • The data retrieved is then transformed into model objects (in lib/models) and passed back to the UI.
   • Custom plugins (lib/plugin) are invoked by both UI and service layers to provide enhanced functionalities such as video playback, popup dialogs, or socket events.
   • External API Services: Even if not maintained internally, a note should be drawn that the mobile client interacts with BiliBili’s API endpoints.

3. Explain Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularization: The clear separation of pages, models, controllers, services, and plugins allows independent development and testing.
   • Layered/MVC Pattern: 
       - The “View” is implemented in Flutter’s UI (pages, widgets)
       - “Controllers” manage user actions and data flows.
       - “Models” represent structured data from API calls.
   • Dependency Injection: (Service Locator in lib/services/service_locator.dart) simplifies testing and enhances modular design.
   • Responsive Design: The project’s multiple directories (android, ios, web, desktop) indicate that the app is built for cross-platform support.

4. Tailor the Diagram for a Full-Stack Mobile Application:
   • Emphasize the distinction between the Flutter app’s presentation layer (UI) and data handling/business logic. For instance, separate blocks labeled “UI/Presentation” and “Business & Data Access.”
   • Include an “External API” block that represents BiliBili (and possibly other third-party services) and show directional arrows between the data access layer and this external entity.
   • Note service integrations for PL (plugin) components that enhance the overall look and functionality.
   • Mention that platform directories (android, ios, etc.) provide native configurations, ensuring that the Flutter code communicates seamlessly with device-specific capabilities.

5. Instruction on Creating the Diagram:
   a. Components and Labels:
      – Create a block for each major component: UI/Presentation (lib/pages, lib/common/widgets), Business Logic/Controllers (lib/pages/*/controller.dart, service_locator), Data Layer (lib/http & lib/models), Plugins (lib/plugin), and External API Services.
      – Draw additional blocks for “Platform-Specific Integrations” to highlight native project files (android, ios, etc.).
   b. Relationships & Data Flows:
      – Use directional arrows to show user interactions: UI triggering controllers, controllers calling data services, and responses being funneled back to update the UI.
      – Show arrows from “Business Logic” to “External API” illustrating outbound HTTP requests (done via the Dio library and similar tools).
   c. Architectural Patterns:
      – Use groupings or color coding (different shapes or colors) to represent the architectural layers (presentation layer, business logic, data, and platform integration).
      – Annotate these with the corresponding technologies (e.g., Flutter for UI, Dart for business logic, Dio for HTTP, dependency injection via service_locator).
   d. Add Extras:
      – Clearly indicate submodules like Video Playback (e.g., pl_player) and Media Gallery (pl_gallery) with distinct symbols or colors.
      – Label each connection (e.g., “Data Fetch”, “User Event”, “Navigation”, “Dependency Injection”).

6. Final Diagram Detailing:
   – Include a legend for colors and shapes.
   – Ensure every component is clearly labeled.
   – Create additional callouts for builds/CI systems (e.g., GitHub Actions, Fastlane) if needed.
   – The high level should not overwhelm minor details – focus on showing how many components collaborate to provide the features listed (e.g., video playback controls, dynamic feed, blacklisting, live streaming support).

Following these guidelines, the resulting diagram will give a comprehensive view of PiliPala’s architecture – clearly outlining how Flutter, service layers, API interactions, and platform-specific code collaborate to create a robust BiliBili third-party client.

This detailed diagram will be an invaluable tool for both onboarding new engineers and clarifying the separation of concerns across the project. Feel free to iterate on the diagram as the project evolves, ensuring the most critical components and interconnections are always captured.
</explanation>
